title: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Shabbat 119a relates that his father Rabbi Abbahu, who was exceedingly wealthy and very pious, had the practice of slaughtering a calf every Saturday night, although he needed only one kidney from it. When Avimi his son grew up, he said to him: “Why do you need all this? Let us leave a kidney from Shabbat eve.” They left it, and a lion came and ate the calf. Avimi his son was very wealthy, and his trade spread in the land, until he traded with the people of Babylonia, with the people of Mechoza, as in Ketubot 85a: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu owed money to the people of Bei Chozai; he sent it through Chama son of Rabbah bar Avuha … the case came before Rabbi Abbahu. Hyman considers it beyond doubt that Avimi went there himself, and this is what we find in Chullin 65b and Niddah 5b: “When Avimi came from Bei Chozai, he brought a baraita with him” (and he considers it unnecessary to posit that Avimi of Bei Chozai is a different person). In Kiddushin 31b his father boasted of him and said: “Such as Avimi my son fulfilled the mitzvah of honoring a father.” It is related there that Avimi had five ordained sons, and when Rabbi Abbahu came and called at the door, Avimi would run and open for him, saying “Yes, yes” until he got there. One day his father asked him to bring him water; before he brought it, he dozed (for his father was old). He bent over him until he woke from his sleep; it happened that he expounded a fine thing on the verse “A psalm of Asaph.”

In the entry Rabbi Abbahu, Hyman remarks that it is a wonder that Avimi’s five ordained sons are not mentioned anywhere, and he proposes there the reading “Rabbi Abbahu had five ordained sons.” Avimi was zealous and was rewarded for honoring his father.

The book Chikrei Lev, part 1, p. 106, says that Avimi was a judge in Caesarea, and its source is Shevuot 42a; but Hyman finds nothing of his there. Likewise what it says there from Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:7, that Rabbi Yonah was in Tyre and heard that Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu had died, and fasted — Hyman accuses it of false testimony, for there they said only that “the son” of Rabbi Abbahu died, and he instead proposes the reading as in Nedarim 1:1, that the son of Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yonah’s colleague, died; Hyman calls this the true reading. Rabbi Abbahu lost only a small child, as stated explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin, end of chapter 6. Hyman considers it very likely that Avimi was the reciter of baraitot in the academy of the Land of Israel, and therefore we always find “Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu taught,” as in Sanhedrin 99a, Avodah Zarah 34b and Chullin 63b.

He is mentioned in Gittin 29b, where he said to the Rabbis: “Let it be a question for you whether he may appoint an agent.” Hyman explains this by saying that in his days there was no longer a head of the academy in the Land of Israel after Rabbi Ami’s death, but only gatherings of sages in Caesarea, Tiberias and Tzippori, as explained in the entry Rabbi Abbahu.

notes.text: Avimi OWES BeiChozai, not the reverse; he sends Hama with payment, then the CASE comes before Abbahu, supported by saved Davidson Ketubot85a and matching returned Hebrew. Five ordained sons is the quotation’s form; Hyman’s proposal shifting them to Abbahu stays explicitly his proposal. His trade/genealogy/death objections and academy-reciter hypothesis remain attributed, without importing a Mishnah-generation claim.

The consulted calf episode is Shabbat 119b, whereas Hyman supplies 119a. It expressly says that the calf was prepared after Shabbat and that Avimi proposed retaining a kidney from Shabbat eve; this supports the body’s Saturday-night wording. Ketubot 85a has Avimi owing Bei Chozai and Hama delivering payment before the resulting case reaches Abbahu. Hyman’s confident identification with Avimi from Bei Chozai and his personal travel inference are not separately established by that debt episode. His transfer of the five ordained sons from Avimi to Abbahu, death-text correction, academy reconstruction and reciter hypothesis remain attributed, with his always assertion preserved.
